title: Over a Bezout domain any unimodular row of length n is the first row of an invertible matrix

standard_prerequisites.name: Bezout domains: finitely generated ideals are principal
standard_prerequisites.use: Allows the ideal generated by the first n - 1 entries to be written as (f) and produces the relation af - b f_n = 1.

standard_prerequisites.name: Invertibility of a matrix with determinant one
standard_prerequisites.use: Certifies that the constructed matrix is invertible.

core_obligations: Note that the statement follows from the earlier splitting lemma but give a direct proof, and argue by induction on n with the case n = 1 immediate (proof lines 37933-37935).
For n > 1, renumber so that f_1 is nonzero, and use the Bezout hypothesis to choose f with (f) = (f_1, ..., f_{n-1}) (proof lines 37936-37937).
By the induction hypothesis applied to the quotients f_1/f, ..., f_{n-1}/f, which generate the unit ideal, take an (n-1) x (n-1) matrix A whose first row is those quotients (proof lines 37938-37939).
Choose a and b with af - b f_n = 1, possible because 1 lies in (f, f_n), and exhibit the explicit product of the two displayed matrices whose first row is f_1, ..., f_n (proof lines 37939-37961).
Observe that the left matrix is invertible because it has determinant 1, so the product is invertible with the required first row, completing the induction (proof lines 37962).
difficulty_reason: The lemma takes a Bezout domain R, an integer n >= 1, and elements f_1, ..., f_n generating the unit ideal, and asserts the existence of an invertible n x n matrix over R whose first row is f_1 ... f_n (source lines 37925-37930). The proof notes that this follows from the earlier splitting lemma but supplies a direct inductive construction. For n = 1 the result holds. For n > 1, after renumbering so that f_1 is nonzero, the proof uses the Bezout hypothesis to choose f with (f) = (f_1, ..., f_{n-1}), takes an (n-1) x (n-1) matrix A whose first row is f_1/f, ..., f_{n-1}/f — which exists by the induction hypothesis, since those quotients generate the unit ideal — and chooses a, b with af - b f_n = 1, possible because 1 lies in (f, f_n) (proof lines 37933-37941). The explicit answer is then the product of the two displayed matrices, the left one having determinant 1 and hence being invertible, whose product therefore has the required first row and is invertible (proof lines 37942-37962). The non-routine content is the reduction of length n to length n - 1 by factoring out the generator of the ideal spanned by the first n - 1 entries, together with the determinant-one matrix that supplies the last column.
